tadābhāsato'nyonyabhidi ca yasmin manovijñāne madhyamātmani antaḥsaṃjalpe, tadrūpatāmaprāpta eva yaḥ prathamaḥ paśyantīśabdavācyaḥ icchālakṣaṇaḥ prasaro yatra pramātṛprameyayoḥ sāmānyarūpatayā api na vivekollāsa iti, etadvastu svayameva nirbhāsate | atra hetumāha yataḥ iti abhinnasya pramātṛprameyarūpasya anunmiṣitavibhāgasya api yadi vastutaḥ prakāśo na syāt, tat tvaritaṃ lipipāṭhe vegasaraṇe tvaritābhidhāne ca (page 170) rekhāto rekhāntaraṃ, deśāt deśāntaraṃ, sthānakaraṇādeḥ sthānakaraṇāntaraṃ ca gacchatastāṃstāṃstyaktavyān grahītavyāṃśca bhāgānnaparāmṛśataḥ [marśataḥ ka. pāṭhaḥ |], tayośca tyāgopādānayoḥ kartāramavimṛ'satastāni [abhimṛśataḥ ka. |] vicitrāṇi tyāgopādānāni kathaṃ bhaveyuḥ parāmarśapūrvakatvena eṣāṃ dṛṣṭatvāt | tadimāni bhavanti svakāraṇaṃ parāmarśamanumāpayanti | naca asau bhedenaiva parāmarśa eṣāmiti | bhedena hi parāmarśe vācikamānasaparispandaparamparāto'bhilāpasaṃketasmaraṇaprabandha- sadbhāve [parasparataḥ kha. |] tvaritataiva na nirvahet | āhaca apohe kvacidvāṅmanasaspandaṃ vinā ityādi | tadayaṃ prayogaḥ- pramātṛprameyaprakāśastyāgopādānayorasti cetanakriyātvāt,- iti kāryahetuḥ | yadasti, naca pṛthak; avaśyaṃ tadapṛthak tṛtīyarāśyabhāvāt, - iti svabhāvahetuḥ | evaṃ vācanadhāvanādi iti grantho'yaṃ pramātṛprameyayorabhedena api asti sadbhāva;- ityetāvati asminnaṃśe hetutayā vyākhyeyaḥ, natu bhuñje gacchāmi ityetadanena spṛśyate iti | tadāhuḥ śrīparameṣṭhipādāḥ yadā tu tasya ciddharmavibhavāmodajṛmbhayā | vicitraracanānānākāryasṛṣṭipravartane || bhavatyunmukhitā cittā secchāyāḥ prathamā tuṭiḥ | (śi. dṛ. 1|8) iti upakramya sā ca dṛśyā hṛduddeśe kāryasmaraṇakālataḥ | praharṣāvedasamaye darasaṃdarśanakṣaṇe || anālocanato dṛṣṭe visargaprasarāspade | visargoktiprasaṅge ca vācane dhāvane tathā || eteṣveva prasaṅgeṣu sarvaśaktivilolatā | iti | atra hi tātparyametat- sarvaśaktiparipūrṇatātmakaṃ cito (page 171) yadrūpam, tat yadā svātantryāt saṃvitsvabhāva āmṛśati tata unmukhībhūtāyāṃ cidrūpatāyāṃ tatprasaraprathama
**The light that knows itself: the heart of the doctrine** Here, in the deepest part of the vimarśa on the knowledge-power, Abhinavagupta states the heart of the whole teaching. The manifestation (prakāśa) is not a passive, inert light. Its very nature is the *reflexive-awareness* (vimarśa) — the light's own grasp of itself. Without the vimarśa, the manifestation would be like crystal: it would show the world, but it would not know that it showed it; it would be inert. What makes the light *light* — what makes it consciousness and not a thing — is that it is aware of itself in the very act of manifesting. Consider the very first surge of knowing. In the inner speech, the middle-self, before the mind has split the knower from the known — in the paśyantī, the seeing, the first stirring of the will — the knower and the known are not yet two, not even by their common form; no distinction has yet flashed. And this, Abhinavagupta says, shines by itself. It is the pure reflexive-awareness before any division. The proof that this is so is drawn from the swiftest of our acts. In quick reading, in rapid motion, in hurried speech, we go from line to line, from place to place, abandoning some things and seizing others — all without pausing to reflect. Yet these abandonments and attainments are, as we see, always preceded by a re-reflection (parāmarśa). They infer their cause, the re-reflection. And that re-reflection cannot be only by the difference of knower and known — for then the very swiftness of the act would fail, tangled in the lineage of speech, mind, motion, convention, memory. The swift act shows that the knower and the known, the abandoning and the attaining, are not two separate things: they are one act of the self-aware consciousness. What is, and is not separate, must be non-separate — there is no third class to hold them apart. And this is the will — the first surge, the first "tuṭi" (the bursting). As the Śivadṛṣṭi says: when the consciousness-dharma, in its splendor and joy, unfolds into the varied creation, and becomes the un-lidded awareness — that is the will's first surge. And she is seen in the sudden moments: in the heart, at the time of remembering an effect, at the moment of rapture or emotion, at the sight of the beloved, at the un-reflected glance, at the very emission of the utterance, in the reading and the running. In all these occasions, the all-power-liveliness of the consciousness flashes. It is the reflexive-awareness, the self-grasping of the light, seen most clearly where the mind does not pause to divide. So the reflexive-awareness is not a thing, not an added quality — it is the manifestation's own nature. The light that shines is the light that knows itself; and this self-knowing is the parā-vāk, the supreme speech, from which all the lower levels of speech (the madhyamā, the vaikharī) descend. It is the Lord's freedom (svātantrya) and his lordship (aiśvarya). This is what Abhinavagupta will draw out in the next kārikās — that consciousness is at once the awareness, its action, and its agency (kārikā 12), and that this reflexive-awareness, the parā-vāk, arising by its own savor, is the supreme freedom of the supreme self (kārikā 13). The heart of the doctrine is here: the light knows itself, and that self-knowing is the Lord. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
